full_judgment:
3. Briefly stated the case of the plaintiff is that the land of Mouza Uttar Amragacia of SA Khatian No. 366 measuring an area of 0.20 decimals sold to defendant Amzad Hossain son of late Khadem Ali Hawlader by registered sale deed dated 27-3-1967 and on the same day an Ekrarnama was executed between the parties to reconvey the said land. This Ekrarnama deed is a Khai Khalashi deed under section 95(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and after promulgation of President Order No.88 of 72 and 136 of 72 land automatically redempt and plaintiff has been possessing the land. It was further stated in the plaint that the plaintiff asked the defendant to execute the return kabala in favour of the plaintiff, but the defendant refused to execute the return kabala finally on 24 Agrahaon, 1412 BS corresponding to 12-12-2005. Thus the plaintiff was constrained to file the present suit. 

 4. The sole defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that the plaintiff sold away '20 decimals of land by registered kabala dated 27-3-1967 and on the same day a deed of reconveyance was executed and registered on 1374 BS for a period of four years and it was stipulated in the reconveyance deed that if the plaintiff refund the kabala value Taka 400 (Four hundred) only, in that case defendant will retransfer the said land but the plaintiff will not get benefit of the President's Order No. 88 of 72 and 136 of 72 and the plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree for redemption of the suit land. With these averments the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 12. It appears that the trial court after considering the evidence and materials on record held that the transaction was a complete usufructuary mortgage and the consideration of which was already specified by the usufruct of the land and since the suit was for redemption of mortgage which was filed within specific period of limitation that is within 60 years and on such finding decreed the suit for redemption and on the other hand on the learned judge of the appellate court held that the transaction was out and out sale and said to be treated as past and closed. It was also found by the appellate court that the seller did not pay the money within the period of four years that is 27-7-1971 when the period of Ekrarnama was expired as such the transaction will be treated as past and closed and the deed will not come within the preview of President's Order No. 88 of 1972. In this respect the appellate court relied on the decision of 32 DLR (AD) 233 but it appears that the appellate court totally misconstrue the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. The appellate court on consideration of the record erroneously found that the present suit is not a mortgage suit as such according to the version of the plaint, the sale deed cannot be treated a deed under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as such same cannot be treated as kot mortgage/Khai Khalashi under President's Order No. 88 of 1972, 136 of 1972 and 34 of 1973 past and closed matter. The appellate court failed to appreciate that the plaintiff filed the present suit for redemption of the mortgage, but the appellate court failed to appreciate and totally misconstrue the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 132 and on such erroneous finding dismissed the suit. 

 13. It further appears that the court of appeal below failed to appreciate that the plaintiff deposited the consideration money Taka 400 on 3-8-2009 after a delay of 75 days. But the court of appeal below erroneously found that the trial court had no jurisdiction to accept the money on 3-8-2009 long after the period fixed in the judgment passed by the trial court, completely overlooking and in not consideration the specific provision of section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure, wherein it was stated that the court may in its discretion, from time to time, enlarge such period, even though the period originally fixed or granted may have expired. 

 15. Before I entering into the merit of the present case let us look into the provision of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Briefly, SAT Act, 1950). Before the amendment made in the year 1969 by the Ordinance No. XX1 of 1969 in section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was 15 years and by this amendment the same period was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgagee does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption under Article 147 of the Limitation Act. In the present case the suit was filed on 9-4-2006 after expiry of 35 years which is well within the period of limitation and same it is not barred by limitation. 

 16. Again section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 has been amended by the President's Order No. 88 of 1972 with effect from 3-8-1972, but this amendment did not touch the period of a usufructuary mortgage which is still 7 (seven) years, nor did it affect the period of limitation for redemption suit which is 60 years. Thus it shows that firstly if, on the expiry of the period of a mortgage, the mortgagee does not restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, then the Sub-divisional Magistrate shall on an application by the mortgagor, restore possession of the mortgagor by evicting the mortgagee. In other words, for getting back possession of a mortgaged land the mortgagor need no file any redemption suit, but may get quick remedy by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. The other provision in the amendment is that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in force, any transfer of land by an out and out sale with a condition for reconveyance shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 (seven) years on the expiry of which the mortgagor may get back possession by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. But since transfer as I have found a mortgage, no question arises whether it should be treated as mortgage. 

 17. It appears from the record of the present case that the sale deed No. 2431 dated 25-3-1967 (Exhibit-A) and four expired on 27-3-1971. President's Order No. 88 of 1972 (Shortly, PO No. 88 of 1972) came into operation on 3-8-1972. Thus it appears that prior to the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 the period of mortgage expired on 27-3-1971. The learned appellate judge wrongly held that the mortgage money was to be paid on or before 27-3-1971 and held that on condition ceased to be operative after promulgation' of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and 136 of 1972 and amendment of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr Md Borhan Uddin, learned Advocate for the opposite-party vehemently argued that section 58C of the Transfer of Property Act will be apply. 

 19. Before parting with the case it may be mentioned that the learned judge of the appellate court took note of the case of Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. The reference of that case in the contention of the present case is wholly irrelevant. The historical background of the legislation is mentioned in PO No. 88 of 1972 in respect of subsisting usufractuary mortgage is hit by section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is meant to protect the helpless raiyat. A raiyat in Bangladesh cannot interfere into any form of usufractuary mortgage other than complete usufractuary mortgage which is capable of enjoyment for a maximum period of seven years and the raiyat will get back his property under section 95 of SAT Act, 1950. 

 20. In this connection the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party although submits on this point, but totally misconceived the respective provision of section 95A and PO No. 88 of 1972. I am afraid that the reference of this case shows total non-application of judicial mind of the learned judge of the appellate court. In this respect in the aforesaid cited case reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 President's Order No. 88 of 1972, President's Order No. 136 of 1972 and President's Order No. 24 of 1973 amending to provision of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and inserting provision of section 95A therein came up for consideration. In that case it was held amongst others "as for the transaction which are not alive before the promulgation of PO No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed." That conclusion was arrived at in view of the contention that an application for restoration of possession of the mortgage land in respect of transaction past and closed was not maintainable. President's Order No. 88 of 1972 created special forum for restoration of mortgaged property. But it did not take away right of redemption available to a mortgagor by filing a mortgage suit under Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter the submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party to that effect is totally erroneous and the view taken by the learned judge of the appellate court are also equally wrong to hold that the suit was not maintainable as the transaction was past and closed.
